summary: A skeletal iron tower at the entrance to Marblehead Harbor: lit since 1835, rebuilt in 1895-96, kept by nine principal keepers, and the 1938 hurricane.

structures.note: 105 ft (32 m) from base to lantern center (USLHS); first lit 17 April 1896
about 23 ft; demolished 1895 to make way for the present tower
date from LighthouseFriends; USLHS lists a brick oil house without a date

access.note: Grounds in Chandler Hovey Park open all year. The lighthouse is open by special arrangement only; the tower is closed (LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard; licensed to the Town of Marblehead

events.note: Eleazer Graves and other residents petition for a lighthouse at the harbor entrance
First exhibited 10 October 1835 (LighthouseFriends); USLHS gives 1835 as year established
Sixth-order Fresnel lens replaces the oil lamps and reflectors
Replacement keeper's dwelling occupied (LighthouseFriends)
Auxiliary light shown from a 100-foot mast near the tower, 10 July 1883
Lighthouse Board asks for a new tower at $45,000
Old brick tower demolished; light moved to a temporary tower on 22 June 1895
Light moved to the new iron tower on the old site, 17 April 1896
Keeper's dwelling connected to the city water supply
Brick oil house added (LighthouseFriends)
Changed to fixed red to set it apart from the town's lights
Electricity reaches the lighthouse; not the keeper's dwelling
Changed to fixed green
Hurricane of 21 September 1938; keeper Harry S. Marden keeps the light going on his car battery
Light goes dark in the Second World War; tower off-limits to the public 1941-1946
Chandler Hovey gives the land around the light to the town for a park
Keeper's dwelling demolished
Light automated
Fresnel lens replaced by a modern optic (300 mm)
Ezekiel Darling and four men bring ashore the crew of the brig John Hancock
Boston Globe credits Keeper James S. Bailey with rescuing seventeen people near the light

corrections.why: The 1835 tower was a brick tower of about 23 ft, demolished in 1895. The skeletal iron tower that stands now was built in 1895 and first lit on 17 April 1896 (NRHP 'Constructed in 1895'; LHB 1896-97 scan p.29).

corrections.proposed: 1896 first_lit of the present tower (or remove)

resolved_conflicts.field: first lit (record's conflict on first years)
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The different first years are two towers, not one disagreement: the brick tower first lit on 10 October 1835 and the present iron skeleton tower first lit on 17 April 1896 (LighthouseFriends; LHB 1896-97 scan p.29).

notes_for_editor: 1) Keeper dates disagree. Roster (USLHS): Martin 1860-1863, Goodwin 1863-1872, Drayton 1893-1925, Eastman 1925-1930. LighthouseFriends text: Goodwin followed Martin in 1862; Drayton took over in 1892 and gave thirty-five years. A bronze plaque at the light, as reported in Wikipedia (lead only, not cited): Martin 1860-1862, Goodwin 1862-1872, Drayton 1893-1928, Eastman 1928-1930, Joseph Barry 1947-1954. Check the plaque on site before any date from it. 2) Land purchase date: NRHP chronology 1833 (with Congress's $4,500 the same year); LighthouseFriends says Congress approved on 30 June 1834 and the purchase followed. Not settled. 3) Brick oil house: LighthouseFriends says 1907; the NRHP major-elements text gives an oil house with a question-marked date of 1835 (OCR is letter-spaced there, so not quoted). 4) Paint: NRHP 1981 chronology (red 1933, green, sandblasted and brown 1980) against LighthouseFriends ('original metallic brown'). 5) Russell B. Eastman: the archive lists him at Marblehead 1925-1930 and at Ned's Point 1914-1923 under one person slug; the same name only. Not linked in the story. 6) Light range: the record's 7 nm is not from any source read here; the NRHP 1981 form says 10 miles. Not used. 7) Current optic 300 mm (USLHS) and the Light List characteristic were not checked against the Light List itself. 8) Second-hand: the 1889 Boston Globe rescues and the 1857 Darling article are cited as quoted by LighthouseFriends; the Chronicling America search for Bailey failed (HTTP 520) and the Drayton search returned nothing, so no newspaper was read directly. 9) The 1835-to-1896 record conflict (first years) is two towers, see resolved_conflicts. 10) Nothing on site was checked; access comes from LighthouseFriends (2026 page) and a virtual guide. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the 1895 entry of the NRHP chronology says the new tower was 'Painted White' before the 1933 red paint; the story now says so. The 1981 date of the form is read from OCR ('July 31, 1981' is not legible in the cached text; the form's own date was not checked on the page image). Mary Drayton's remark and the 1857 and 1889 newspaper passages are used only as LighthouseFriends prints them (footnoted to LighthouseFriends). The 1893 'new tower 45,000' line is from the Board's appropriation list (scan 44) and the brick-tower proposal is scan 66 in the same volume; the 1894 report (scan 362) says the proposal 'is renewed'.
